Some attribute this saying to the Islamic period. (Publisher.) Others attribute it specifically to the Prophet and to Imam Ali. It is said that “the green plant on a dunghill” means a beautiful woman of bad origin and character.↩︎

“The green plant on a dunghill”: one meaning of dimna is a rubbish heap. Its “green plant” is the grass that grows there thick and fresh. The expression therefore describes outward beauty hiding the filth of its place of growth. The proverb warns against being deceived by an attractive surface that conceals something bad underneath. It reflects botanical observation generalized into a social rule.↩︎

al-Ajza’ here means a raised hill of sand too barren to produce plants. The proverb is used when good comes from someone from whom good was not expected, just as one does not expect fertility or lush growth from such barren ground.↩︎
The ostrich is a bird of the ostrich family. This proverb is used of someone who has no distinct color, position, or opinion of his own.↩︎
This proverb means that miserliness does not come from a person’s nature but from lack of means. It expresses a social view.↩︎
Khalla means need and poverty; salla means secret theft. The proverb therefore says that theft is produced by poverty. Here too we find an advanced way of thinking about a social problem.↩︎

This proverb lays down a rule about punishment that is the same in principle as the rule later expressed in the Qur’anic verse, “In retaliation there is life for you, people of understanding.” The pre-Islamic proverb says that executing murderers in retaliation is the way to remove murder from society.↩︎

This proverb resembles the previous one because it also provides the basis for a legal rule: a person who abandons someone and thereby causes his death is equal to the killer—in other words, he is a partner in the killing.↩︎

This proverb expresses the idea that similarity between things in some outward features does not mean that they agree in all their other characteristics. Recognizing the logic of this proverb is important from the standpoint of knowledge.↩︎

Ukaz was a place between Ta’if and Nakhla on the road to Mecca. As the pilgrimage season approached, the pre-Islamic Arabs would go there and hold a market from the first of Dhu al-Qa‘da until the twentieth. They then moved to Dhu al-Majanna, where another market was held, and from there to Dhu al-Majaz for a third market. On the eighth of Dhu al-Hijja, pilgrims began moving toward Mecca. Ukaz was distinctive because people came from every part and edge of the Arabian Peninsula to trade, exchange or ransom prisoners, and hold gatherings for tribal boasting. Poetry was often recited as part of this boasting. See al-Aghani, vol. 2; Yaqut al-Hamawi, Dictionary of Countries, entry “Ukaz”; and other sources and studies.↩︎

The story tells of two angels who descended to earth and were captivated by the beauty of a woman named al-Zuhra, Venus. They taught her the words by which they ascended to heaven. When she herself ascended, she forgot the words by which she could descend to earth, so she remained there and became the beautiful planet that the pre-Islamic Arabs associated with music, pleasure, and amusement.
